The butterfly collecting season around Reading lasts six weeks in late summer. (See graph below.) If you’re going to chase them one by one, you won’t catch very many. So the next step for Ebright was to raise a flock of butterflies. He would catch a female monarch, take her eggs, and raise them in his basement through their life cycle, from egg to caterpillar to pupa to adult butterfly. Then he would tag the butterflies’ wings and let them go. For several years his basement was home to thousands of monarchs in different stages of development.

Choose the option that best explains why Ebright changed the way he collected monarch butterflies. (A) raising them gave him thousands of monarchs at different stages of development (B) the monarchs near Reading could not be caught at all once the season began (C) Dr Urquhart asked him to raise monarchs instead of tagging them outdoors (D) chasing the butterflies one by one would not give him very many

answerScheme.modelAnswer: chasing the butterflies one by one would not give him very many

questions.subject: English
questions.stem: Your school is holding a one-day Science Exhibition next month and every student of Classes 9 and 10 may enter one project of his or her own. Write a notice for the school notice board giving the theme of the exhibition, what each entrant must display and the last date for entries. (100 words)

markingPoints.description: Content: the notice gives the theme of the exhibition, who may enter, what each entrant must display and the last date for entries
Format: a capitalised heading for a notice board, the body in clear short paragraphs and the issuing authority at the end
Organisation: the details are arranged in a sensible order, that is, what is being held, who may join, what to display and how to enrol
Accuracy: correct spelling, punctuation, capital letters and a formal and concise tone suitable for a school notice board
Expression: simple sentences and suitable vocabulary that persuade students to bring a real experiment

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
SCIENCE EXHIBITION — SCHOOL NOTICE BOARD

Calling all students of Classes 9 and 10. The Annual Science Exhibition will be held in the school hall next month. Every entrant must display one project of his or her own work. Please put up a short note on the board used, the material needed and the time the work took. Entries will be closed on the last working day of this month. Projects that show real experiments and not only neat displays will be given priority. Enrol at the science laboratory during the lunch break. Come and make our exhibition worth visiting.

evidence: He realised the winners had tried to do real experiments, not simply make a neat display.

questions.subject: English
questions.stem: At an assembly for Classes 9 and 10 you have to speak on the value of asking questions. Write a speech of about 100 words on the topic, “Why the questions we ask are the beginning of science.”

markingPoints.description: Content: the speech says clearly that the questions children ask are the beginning of scientific inquiry
Format: a salutation to the audience, the body of the speech and a concluding thank you
Organisation: a clear beginning, a middle part that gives everyday examples of wondering, and a short conclusion that sums up the message
Accuracy: correct spelling, punctuation, capital letters and a formal tone suitable for a school assembly
Expression: simple sentences and suitable vocabulary that hold the attention of the audience

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
Honourable Principal, teachers and dear friends,

I want to speak for a few minutes on a simple habit: asking questions. Children everywhere wonder about the world around them, and the questions they ask are the beginning of scientific inquiry. A boy who collects things and then asks what they are, or a child who asks why the rain falls in drops, has already taken the first step. So never be afraid to say, “I do not know, but I want to find out.” Curiosity is a cheap quality, and once you begin to ask questions, it stays with you.

Thank you.

evidence: Children everywhere wonder about the world around them.
The questions they ask are the beginning of scientific inquiry.
You also must have wondered about certain things around you.

Organisation: the situation comes first, then what has already been tried, and the request comes last, in clear paragraphs
Accuracy: correct spelling, punctuation, capital letters and a polite, formal tone suitable for a request to a scientist
Expression: short, clear and to the point sentences that explain the request without repetition

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
To: The Scientist, Entomology Laboratory
Subject: Request for suggestions for a science project

Respected Sir/Madam,

I am a student of Class 10 and my school fair is next month. I want to test a theory about a plant that grows in my own garden, but I do not know how to begin. So far I have only prepared a neat display of pressed leaves. Could you suggest one experiment I can carry out in a small garden and tell me which materials I would need? I shall be grateful for any advice.

Yours obediently,
A student of Class 10

When he saw those photos, Ebright didn’t shout, ‘Eureka!’ or even, ‘I’ve got it!’ But he believed that, along with his findings about insect hormones, the photos gave him the answer to one of biology’s puzzles: how the cell can ‘read’ the blueprint of its DNA. DNA is the substance in the nucleus of a cell that controls heredity. It determines the form and function of the cell. Thus DNA is the blueprint for life.

questions.subject: English
questions.stem: Trace, step by step, the chain of events that carried Richard Ebright from reading about monarch migration as a small boy to a theory about the life of cells.

markingPoints.description: His mother gave him the book The Travels of Monarch X, which told how monarchs migrate to Central America and opened the world of science to him
The book invited readers to tag butterflies for research by Dr Frederick A. Urquhart of the University of Toronto, Canada, and his mother wrote to him
He attached light adhesive tags to the wings of monarchs and raised a flock in his basement because the season lasts only six weeks
He lost a county science fair in the seventh grade and learnt that the winners had tried to do real experiments, not simply make a neat display
He wrote to Dr Urquhart for ideas, and the suggestions kept him busy all through high school
In his second year in high school he began the work on the twelve gold spots which led to his theory on the life of cells

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
1. His mother gave him The Travels of Monarch X, which told how monarchs migrate to Central America and opened the world of science to him.
2. The book asked readers to tag butterflies for Dr Urquhart of the University of Toronto, Canada, and his mother wrote to him.
3. He tagged monarchs and, as the season lasts six weeks, raised a flock in his basement from egg to adult.
4. In the seventh grade he lost a county science fair and learnt that the winners had done real experiments.
5. He wrote to Dr Urquhart for ideas, and they kept him busy all through high school.
6. In his second year in high school he began work on the twelve gold spots of a monarch pupa, which led to his theory on the life of cells.

evidence: “But then my mother got me a children’s book called The Travels of Monarch X.”
At the end of the book, readers were invited to help study butterfly migrations.
In his second year in high school, Richard Ebright began the research that led to his discovery of an unknown insect hormone.

questions.subject: English
questions.stem: Explain, step by step, how Richard Ebright’s question about the gold spots on a monarch pupa led to a hormone, to a knowledge of its chemical structure, and finally to his new theory about how a cell reads DNA.

markingPoints.description: His question was what the purpose of the twelve tiny gold spots on a monarch pupa was, and Dr Urquhart did not believe the spots were only ornamental
He and another science student built a device showing that the spots produced a hormone necessary for the butterfly’s full development
The project won first place in the county fair and third place for zoology at the International Science and Engineering Fair
As a high school junior he continued advanced experiments on the pupa and won first place at the International Science Fair
In his senior year he grew cells from a monarch’s wing which divided into normal wing scales only if fed the hormone, and later identified the hormone’s chemical structure
A year-and-a-half later the X-ray photos of that structure gave him the idea for his theory about how the cell reads the blueprint of its DNA

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
1. His question was simple: what is the purpose of the twelve tiny gold spots on a monarch pupa? Dr Urquhart did not believe they were ornamental.
2. He and another science student built a device showing that the spots produced a hormone necessary for the butterfly’s full development.
3. That project won first place in the county fair and third for zoology at the International Fair.
4. As a junior he continued advanced experiments on the pupa and won first place at the International Science Fair.
5. In his senior year he grew cells from a monarch’s wing which divided into normal wing scales only if fed the hormone.
6. The next summer he identified the hormone’s chemical structure, and X-ray photos of it later gave him his theory of how a cell reads DNA.

evidence: The question he tried to answer was simple: What is the purpose of the twelve tiny gold spots on a monarch pupa?
“Everyone assumed the spots were just ornamental,” Ebright said. “But Dr Urquhart didn’t believe it.”
Using the laboratory’s sophisticated instruments, he was able to identify the hormone’s chemical structure.

questions.subject: English
questions.stem: Richard Ebright became a scientist without giving up his other interests. Explain, step by step, what he had as a young boy, what his mother added, how losing a science fair changed his work, and what his teacher says he was really after.

markingPoints.description: An only child, he grew up north of Reading, Pennsylvania, and from kindergarten he collected butterflies, rocks, fossils and coins
He was an eager astronomer, star-gazing all night, and he earned top grades in school
His mother encouraged his interest, bought him equipment and gave him learning work at the dining room table
In the seventh grade he lost a county science fair and learnt that the winners had done real experiments
He wrote to Dr Urquhart for ideas and the suggestions led to prize projects and then to his theory on the life of cells
He stayed a debater, public speaker, canoeist and photographer, and was competitive only because he wanted to do the best job he could

answerScheme.modelAnswer:
1. An only child, he grew up north of Reading, Pennsylvania, and from kindergarten collected butterflies, rocks, fossils and coins.
2. He was an eager astronomer, sometimes star-gazing all night, and he earned top grades in school.
3. His mother encouraged his interest in learning, bought him equipment, and gave him learning work at the dining room table.
4. In the seventh grade he lost a county science fair and learnt that the winners had tried real experiments.
5. He wrote to Dr Urquhart for ideas, and they led to prize projects and then to his theory on the life of cells.
6. He stayed a champion debater, public speaker, canoeist and photographer, and was competitive only because he wanted to do the best job he could.

evidence: An only child, Ebright grew up north of Reading, Pennsylvania.
“There wasn’t much I could do there,” he said. “I certainly couldn’t play football or baseball with a team of one. But there was one thing I could do — collect things.”
For the right reasons, he wants to be the best.
